title: Two Prophets, One Broken Yoke
overview: A prophet named Hananiah publicly contradicts Jeremiah by promising a quick end to Babylon's rule, and the chapter shows how their clash plays out.

parts.label: Hananiah's hopeful promise (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: In the temple, in front of priests and crowds, Hananiah announces that within two years the LORD will break Babylon's power and bring back the stolen temple treasures, the exiled king Jehoiachin and the other captives. This flatly contradicted Jeremiah, who had been wearing a wooden yoke on his neck as a sign that Judah and the nations around it should submit to Babylon.

parts.label: Jeremiah's 'Amen' and test (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: Jeremiah says he wishes it were true, which shows he took no pleasure in his own grim message. But he points out that earlier prophets had warned of war and disaster, and a prophet who promises peace is only proven right when it actually happens.

parts.label: The yoke smashed (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: Hananiah pulls the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it, a public counter sign meant to show Babylon's grip being broken. Jeremiah simply walks away, apparently choosing not to argue until he had a reply from the LORD.

parts.label: Wood replaced by iron (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: The answer comes: breaking a wooden yoke only brings an iron one, meaning that resisting Babylon would lead to harsher rule, not freedom. Saying even the wild animals are under Babylon's king pictures how complete his control would be.

parts.label: Hananiah's death (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: Jeremiah tells Hananiah the LORD did not send him, that he has led people to trust a lie and urged rebellion against God, and that he will die that year. The text records bluntly that he died two months later, presenting it as judgment and offering no softer explanation.

think: When two confident voices promise you very different futures, what actually makes you trust one over the other?
